Soccer Data Science Challenge: Foul-Winning Probability Model¶

Name: Caio Rosa Rocha
Project: Swish Analytics Soccer Challenge
Date: June 2026

This project builds a model to estimate the probability that a player wins a foul after a Ball Receipt or Ball Recovery event using EPL event data.¶

Data Reading & Inspection: EPL Event Data¶

mask = df["type.name"].isin(["Ball Recovery", "Ball Receipt*"])

start_types = ["Ball Recovery", "Ball Receipt*"]

starts = df.loc[mask].copy()

In [11]:
# Initializing the target column
starts["foul_won"] = 0

# Looping each Foul Won event backwards, so that we can flag the rows in which a foul was won after Receipt/Recovery

for (match_id, possession), group in possession_groups:
   
    group = group.sort_values("index") # Sort index to get the correct order of action on a possession
    foul_rows = group[group["type.name"] == "Foul Won"] # Keeping only the rows that have a foul won action
    if foul_rows.empty:
        continue

    for _, foul in foul_rows.iterrows():
        foul_player = foul["player.name"] # Capture name of player fouled
        foul_index = foul["index"] # Capture index of the action inside the possession

        previous_events = group[group["index"] < foul_index] # Looking at indexes before foul, accessing the possession backwards

        previous_starts = previous_events[(previous_events["type.name"].isin(start_types)) & # start_types = ["Ball Recovery", "Ball Receipt*"]
                                          (previous_events["player.name"] == foul_player)] # Find previous Ball Receipt/Recovery by the same player who won the foul

        if not previous_starts.empty:
            start_df_index = previous_starts.tail(1).index[0] # Getting the most recent reception/recovery by the same player
            starts.loc[start_df_index, "foul_won"] = 1 # Labeling the foul

# This label assumes that the closest previous Ball Receipt or Ball Recovery by the same player within 
# the same possession represents the start of the player’s foul-winning possession.

# Categorizing different areas of the pitch

# Max value for horizontal pitch size is 120

              (model_df["x"] >= 40) & (model_df["x"] < 80),
              model_df["x"] >= 80]

model_df["pitch_area_x"] = np.select(conditions_x, choices_x, default = "unknown")

# Max value for vertical pitch size is 80,

The spatial distribution shows that actions are more concentrated in the middle areas of the pitch along X (horizontally). Along Y (vertically), actions appear more frequent in the wider areas than in the central channel.¶
The number of actions is pretty even throughout the game, with an increase during the middle of the match.¶
Around 9.13% of actions happened while players were under pressure.¶

The average location for events that led to a foul won was around x = 61.4 and y = 39.7. Since the pitch coordinates range from 0 to 120 on the x-axis and 0 to 80 on the y-axis, this suggests that foul-winning events are concentrated around the central area of the pitch.¶
The average time in which a foul is won is around the middle of the game, as match has around 5500 to 6000 seconds.¶
The biggest difference between rates of fouls is being under pressure. Around 36.8% of events that were under pressure led to a foul, while only around 8.6% of non-foul events were under pressure. This suggests that being under pressure is strongly associated with fouls.¶

The binned analysis is probably the most informative one thus far. For each bin, time or location, we can see the number of occurances and how often did fouls happen inside each interval. Since foul_won is a binary variable, the mean is the rate in which a foul happened.¶
For X (horizontal; 0-120), fouls happened more often between 36.07 and 84.03. This is the middle of the pitch, in which physical battle happen often and with less danger to close free kicks. The rate decreases singificantly near the attacking goal. This suggests that pitch depth is related to foul-winning probability.¶
For Y (Vertical, 0-80), fouls happen way more often on the extremes of the pitch. They happen more often between 0 and 16 & 64 and 80. The extremities are also areas in which the goal is further away, so it is less harmful to foul, and the sidelines limits space between actions and players.¶
Time is interesting. The further into the match, rates increase. This can show that players are more tired and commit more fouls by being physical but more reckless.¶

Main Findings:¶
  • Categorical analysis matches the numerical analysis: Many numerical findings appear again in the categorical analysis.
  • Ball Recovery is twice as likely to lead to a foul than ball reception.
  • Middle of the pitch is the most likely area for a foul to occur.
  • The sides of the pitch also have a higher foul rate than the center.
  • The position of players play a large role, as attacking players have a higher likelihood of receiving a foul than defensive players.
  • Second-half events have slightly higher foul rates

# Importing necessary libraries for a logistic regression and preprocessing to fit the model
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
In [36]:
# Separating numerical features by continuous and binary (for scaling)

continuous_features = ["x", "y", "time_seconds"]
binary_features = ["under_pressure_clean"]
categorical_features = categorical_variables
In [37]:
# Creating the preprocessor

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(transformers = [("continuous", StandardScaler(), continuous_features), 
                                                 ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
                                                 ("binary", "passthrough", binary_features)])
In [38]:
# Creating the pipeline

log_reg_pipeline = Pipeline(steps = [("preprocessor", preprocessor), ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
In [39]:

Model Evaluation: Probability Quality and Performance¶

In [41]:
# Probability prediciton for foul_won = 1

y_pred_probability = log_reg_pipeline.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_pred_probability[:10]
Out[41]:
array([0.00999708, 0.01579569, 0.01510451, 0.01557721, 0.00313112,
       0.01264088, 0.01383812, 0.0164354 , 0.00898192, 0.0070916 ])
These 10 probabilities are a peek of the range in which the probabilities can reach. As foul_won = 1 is a rare event which occured only 1.7% of the time, low probabilities are coherent to the scope of the target.¶
In [42]:
# Evaluating probability quality and ranking performance
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, log_loss, brier_score_loss

roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_pred_probability)
logloss = log_loss(y_test, y_pred_probability)
brier = brier_score_loss(y_test, y_pred_probability)

print("ROC AUC:", roc_auc)
print("Log Loss:", logloss)
print("Brier Score:",brier)

ROC AUC: 0.7651081680847781
Log Loss: 0.07991419789134856
Brier Score: 0.016923466473266424

Interpretation:¶

ROC AUC measures how well the model ranks foul-winning events. A value above 0.50 means that the model evaluates the probabilities better than randomly guessing foul_won. Since the target is very imbalanced, the model does not need high probabilities but accurate ranking.¶
Log Loss measures if a model is confidently getting the wrong answer or not. If it is, log loss becomes an incredibly high number. Since log loss is very small (around 0.07), it states that the model is doing a good job in predicting realistic probabilites and it is not being confidently wrong.¶
Brier Score calculates the overall precision of the prediceted probabilities, line by line. It is useful to fine tune the model and see if the probabilities are linearly and significantly different.¶
In this dataset, in which fouls are a rare event, ROC AUC is the main indicator of success. While having small log loss and Brier scores, since the data is very imbalanced (1.7% of foul_won = 1), if the model predicted all 0s, log loss and Brier would be small nontheless. ROC AUC states that we have 76.5% of chance of attributing a more correct probability to a foul event rather than a non-foul event. It is possible to say that the model is learning from the data, and that it is understanding what situation generates a foul.¶
In [43]:
# Baseline Probabilities to compare metrics

baseline_prob = y_train.mean()

baseline_pred = np.full_like(y_test, fill_value=baseline_prob, dtype=float)

baseline_logloss = log_loss(y_test, baseline_pred)
baseline_brier = brier_score_loss(y_test, baseline_pred)

print("Baseline Log Loss:", baseline_logloss)
print("Baseline Brier Score:", baseline_brier)

Baseline Log Loss: 0.08896361901369296

Here, a comparison was made to the baseline porbabilities, and log loss and Brier Score were small. This does not informs much, as the foul_won = 1 event is very rare.¶

Feature Engineering Addition + Random Forest/XGBoost modeling¶

The initial model was interesting and the ROC AUC results portrayed that, but there is room for improvement. Two additional features are going to be added and Random Forest & XGBoost models are going to be used.¶

The ROC AUC increased compared to the logistic regression model, which suggests that the Random Forest improved the model’s ranking performance. Since ROC AUC measures how well the model separates foul-winning events from non-foul events, this improvement indicates that the Random Forest is learning useful patterns from the features and performing better than random guessing.¶
The Average Precision metric showed that the model is around 4.5x (0.0807/0.0177 ≈ 4.56) better than just randomly ranking foul events. This is especially meaningful, as we can confidently say that the model is capable of concentrating real fouls near the top of the predicted-probability ranking. The result looks small (0.0807), but, since the target rate (0.0177) is very small, this value makes sense.¶

This project aimed to create a model that predicted the probability that a player would win a foul when a player received or recovered the ball. Since foul events are rare, accuracy was not the main metric used to evaluate the models. The models were evaluated using ROC AUC, Log Loss, Average Precision and Brier Score.¶
The EDA showed that foul-winning probability changes depending on event context. Events under pressure, Ball Recovery, pitch zones, player position and counterattacks were associated with higher foul-winning rates.¶
By the features table, we can see that the under pressure feature was the most important feature in the XGBoost model by far, followed by Counter attacks, Ball Recovery and Final Third. Remembering that feature importance does not necesserily imply causation, but what the model used the most to evaluate probabilities.¶
Pitch area and position also play an important part in foul-winning rates, as some positions engage in more physical battles and some pitch areas have less goal danger.¶
Overall, the feature-importance analysis' results are consistent to the EDA. The XGBoost seemed to rely on events such as pressure, play patterns, event type, pitch area and player position.¶
